question: According to Regulation (EU) No 1169/20111, the provision of food information shall provide a basis for final consumers to make informed choices and to make safe use of food, also with regard to social and ethical considerations.

According to the judgment of the Court of Justice of the EU in case C-363/18, the Commission must ensure EU consumers’ rights to be adequately informed when products are imported from Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories (OPTs).

Moreover, if mislabelled, a product coming from an Israeli settlement in the OPTs would illegally be granted the preferential tariff treatment set out in the EU-Israel Association Agreement. In light of all of the above: 1.
What are the customs practices when goods from settlements are presented for release for free circulation without proper labelling, or when there is a suspicion that the labelling is misleading?

Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2011 on the provision of food information to consumers, amending Regulations (EC) No 1924/2006 and (EC) No 1925/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council, and repealing Commission Directive 87/250/EEC, Council Directive 90/496/EEC, Commission Directive 1999/10/EC, Directive 2000/13/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council, Commission Directives 2002/67/EC and 2008/5/EC and Commission Regulation (EC) No 608/2004 (OJ L 304, 22.
11.2011, p. 18, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/1169/oj).

Do customs authorities of EU Member States have the tools to communicate, in their daily notifications to the Commission about products released for free circulation, that some of them come from Israeli settlements in the OPTs?
Would deliberate mislabelling practices, and the resulting subsequent fraudulent access to the preferential tariff treatment, trigger the suspension of the EU-Israel Association Agreement?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.7.2026) 1. To determine whether goods are entitled to preferential treatment under the EU Israel Association Agreement, customs authorities apply the rules contained in that Agreement´s Protocol on Origin and in the ‘Technical Arrangement’ adopted in 2005.

The operation of that arrangement has been described in previous Commission replies1 and relies on information contained in proofs of preferential origin rather than on that contained in product labels.

Regulation 1169/2011 on the provision of food information to consumers sets certain rules on the indication of the origin of food products, making such indication mandatory for certain products and for certain cases in which the non-indication of origin would be misleading. Where the indication is provided, it must be accurate.
As a rule, the indications of origin in the labels are incumbent on ‘food business operators’ which are subject to the control by food authorities.

Where sectors or products for which marketing standards are established under Regulation 1308/2013 on the Common Market Organisation are concerned, products not meeting those standards are not allowed to be marketed within the EU and need to be brought into conformity prior to their placing on the market.

Where conformity checks identify possible fraudulent or deceptive practices in respect of the marketing standards, competent authorities should take appropriate action in accordance with the Official Controls Regulation2 and exchange fraud notifications in accordance with Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/17153. 2. No, the Customs Surveillance system4 cannot be used for that purpose. 3.

For the reasons described in the answer to question 1, the sole fact that food originating in the Israeli settlements in the Occupied Palestinian territories is mislabelled as originating in Israel when presented to EU consumers, does not necessarily entail that the food in question has received preferential treatment upon its importation.
